k-1.x_notes: Problems 1-5 are the same as Y's, and the mathematics checks out. P1 mixes coverable boards (hexagon, 2x2 parallelogram, chevron) with ones that cannot be covered: two have odd area, and the side-2 triangle and the 8-triangle trapezoid have even area but are blocked by the up/down count. P2: fewest greens on triangles of side 2, 3, 4 (answers 2, 3, 4). P3: all coverings of the small hexagon (2) and the 1-2-1 hexagon (3), with spare boards. P4: fewest blocks (3, 3, 4), which is not trivial. P5: a blue-block placement game (first, second, first, first, second). All boards are actual size, the wording is plain, and there is plenty of hands-on work. P6 (all 6 coverings of the 1-2-2 hexagon) gives eight actual-size boards across two pages, so children build each covering with blocks and leave it in place to compare. This stays fully concrete and matches P3. Weaknesses: page 7 is an unlabeled continuation page, and P6 needs about 48 blue blocks at one table.
k-1.y_notes: Problems 1-5 match X's word for word. The material is strong and correct, at actual size, with good variety and enough work for the full time. P6 gives one large board for building and eight half-size outlines, and children must draw each covering on a small outline. That is a sensible way to record and compare, and it fits on one page. But kindergartners and first graders drawing rhombus tilings on half-inch grids will be slow and inaccurate, and they will need adult help. This is less concrete than building each covering and leaving it in place.
k-1.reason: The packets are identical except for Problem 6. There X keeps K-1 children building every covering with blocks on actual-size boards, while Y asks very young children to draw tilings on small outlines.

grades-2-3.x_notes: The boards, diagrams and problem sequence are the same as Y's, and all are correct. P1 and P2 mix boards that can be covered (the star, the 2-1-1 hexagon, G) with impossible ones: B has odd area, C and E are blocked by the up/down count, and F is the bowtie, where the counts balance but it is still impossible. Next come the fewest-gap triangles of sides 2-5, the generalization to sides 10 and 100, and the chevron comparison (chevrons never beat blues and do worse on sides 2 and 3). The last two problems are designing a 20-triangle board that needs 6 greens, and a rule for which two green triangles let blues cover a side-2 hexagon. Small advantages: P3 says the four triangles are 'on this page and the next page', which ties the unlabeled page 4 to the problem, and P4 asks 'Explain how you know', which fits a problem whose substance is the general argument.
grades-2-3.y_notes: The content is identical to X and equally strong and correct. P3 says only 'each big triangle', so a child may not realize the side-5 triangle on the unlabeled page 4 belongs to it. 'The biggest triangle' could then be read as the side-4 triangle. P4 asks only for the numbers and leaves the justification to the adult.
grades-2-3.reason: The packets are the same except for two phrases. X's pointer to the next page and its request for a justification in Problem 4 make it marginally clearer to work from independently.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Problems 1-6 are the same as Y's, apart from wording. The sequence is: coverings of the 1-2-2 hexagon (6), the flip graph (greatest distance 4), shortest flip routes on the side-2 hexagon, the parity of closed flip loops (4 flips works; 5 and 7 are impossible), ribbons, and the proof that every round trip is even. Two wording points help: P5 says 'the hexagon board from Problem 3', which separates it from Problem 1's hexagon. P6 asks children to find the fewest flips from E to F and prove nobody can do better, so it does not depend on their earlier answer being optimal. P7 is the 1-3-3 board, where one ribbon gives C(6,3) = 20 coverings, the direct use of the ribbon idea. P8 then counts the coverings of the side-2 hexagon (also 20), which needs two ribbons. This order runs from easy to hard.
grades-4-5.y_notes: The material is the same and equally correct. P6 asks children to explain why nobody can beat 'your answer' from Problem 3, which asks them to prove something false if their earlier answer was not optimal. P5 says only 'the hexagon board', which is ambiguous because Problem 1's board is also a hexagon. Problems 7 and 8 come in the reverse order: children first draw all 20 coverings of the side-2 hexagon (the two-ribbon case) and only then meet the single-ribbon 1-3-3 board, which is the natural next step after Problem 5.
grades-4-5.reason: X has the same problems in a better order (one ribbon before two), plus two small wording improvements. Y's problems could be reordered in a few minutes.

overall.reason: The two packets are nearly identical, and both have correct, substantial, well-sized material in all three bands. X is marginally better in each band: it keeps K-1 building every covering with blocks, its 2-3 cross-references are clearer, and its 4-5 ribbon problems come in a better order with more robust wording. None of Y's weaknesses would cause real trouble in class, and all are quick to edit.
